sidequest-1.title: Welcome to the jungle
sidequest-1.subtitle: An immersive installation that transforms a static canvas into a dynamic narrative window, encouraging viewers to connect with art beyond its context.
sidequest-1.description: A group of friends goes to a museum to see the famous paintings. None of the art has explanation signs, but that doesn't stop them. Soon, they find a painting of a jungle. As they stare at it and imagine what it means, the picture suddenly seems to come to life! They all get super excited and start sharing their own fun ideas about it. Feeling inspired, they move on to look at the next unknown painting, ready to use their imaginations again.
sidequest-1.challenge: Visitors often find it difficult to appreciate museum art when there is no context or description provided, leading to a lack of connection with the piece. The primary challenge was to bridge this gap by creating an immersive experience that encourages viewers to engage with unfamiliar art, even when they lack background information on the artist or the painting’s history.
sidequest-1.tools: Mad Mapper, Photoshop, After Effects, Ableton Live
sidequest-1.client: Minor Audio & Visual Design, Hogeschool Utrecht

processVideos.caption: Process video showing the first motion test for the projection-mapped canvas.
Process video documenting the narrative movement and audio timing in the scene.

sidequest-1.process: My process began with digital research, drawing inspiration from projection mapping artists on Behance and TikTok. To animate the static image, I deconstructed the painting in Photoshop, creating distinct layers for elements like plants to ensure fluid movement. I experimented with narrative techniques, integrating ambient jungle sounds and constructing a physical museum scene around the canvas. Following feedback from a Mini-Expo that highlighted the need for a stronger, clearer storyline, I refined the project by developing a narrative centered on a group of friends visiting a museum, allowing the audience to follow their journey through the visuals and audio.

processImages.caption: Digital Copy of the physical painting

processImages.contextText: Deconstructed painting in Photoshop to create layers for animation

sidequest-1.results: The final installation creates an immersive environment where the painted elements come to life, inviting the audience to form their own interpretations of the artwork. By showing that stories can be communicated through movement and audio in the absence of traditional descriptions, the project encourages museum-goers to continue exploring unfamiliar art with greater confidence.

sidequest-2.title: Borderland Subversion
sidequest-2.subtitle: An immersive art installation challenging perspectives on immigration and the manipulative nature of contextual information.
sidequest-2.role: Creative Research, Concept Development and Design
sidequest-2.description: Borderland Subversion is an impactful art installation inspired by Carlos Barrias's photograph of Maria Hernandez’s immigration journey. The work explores the emotional separation of families and the systemic challenges faced by those seeking a better life. By using a symbolic curtain as a border wall and immersive light projections, the installation forces viewers to confront how selectively displayed information, and the idea that the grass is always greener on the other side, can manipulate our moral choices and assumptions about immigration.
sidequest-2.challenge: The core challenge was to prompt viewers to reflect on their own biases regarding immigration while highlighting how information can be misleading when presented out of context. Inspired by the philosophical trolley problem, the goal was to avoid creating a good or bad side, instead forcing participants to grapple with the difficulty of resolving moral dilemmas. We aimed to move beyond static observation and create an environment where the audience’s own decision to engage with the other side revealed their internal reliance on manipulated narratives.
sidequest-2.client: Minor Audio & Visual Design, Hogeschool Utrecht
sidequest-2.process: Our process was highly iterative, beginning with broad creative research using the 2023 World Press Photo contest as a foundation to identify themes of displacement and trauma. We moved from initial abstract concepts involving the trolley problem to a concrete, anchored narrative based on the real-life journey of Maria Hernandez. Throughout the project, we developed five distinct prototypes; each stage involved significant physical and digital testing, such as simulating the exhibition space with scale models and exploring spatial layouts using curtains and projectors. We learned to adapt our vision to physical constraints, such as shifting from a door-based concept to a curtain-gap design, and we utilized MadMapper to project animated paths that guided visitors through the space. We also made the intentional choice to exclude audio, concluding after testing that the visual and textual elements were powerful enough on their own and that sound would have been a distracting, unnecessary addition.

processImages.caption: First prototype testing the adapted trolley problem concept

processVideos.caption: Assets of the final installation, including the curtain gap and projected animated paths.

sidequest-2.results: The final installation realized a two-sided immersive experience that uses contrasting colors, orange and blue, to represent two worlds without imposing moral judgment. By guiding visitors through a curtain gap using animated zipper and stripe effects, the installation prompted them to physically move between perspectives, mirroring the difficult choices faced by migrants. Feedback from the final exhibition indicated that the concept was clear and effective, with the simplicity of the design cited as a key strength. The project met its primary goal by encouraging visitors to examine how context shapes decisions and to leave with a more critical understanding of the complex, systemic, and emotional realities of emigration.

sidequest-3.title: Techno Albert Heijn
sidequest-3.subtitle: A sound landscape is a short audio piece where you construct a new audio fragment using existing individual sounds, self-recorded sounds, and music. I accomplished this by making decisions about the timing and applied effects on all the fragments. Here is the end result that you can listen to.
sidequest-3.description: An immersive audio-visual exploration mapping the everyday auditory environment of a supermarket into an electronic soundscape. By taking mundane, routine sounds-such as register beeps, fridge hums, and rustling packaging-the project reconstructs them into a rhythmic narrative. A soundscape is an acoustic environment or combination of sounds that forms an immersive audio atmosphere, transforming passive ambient noise into an active storytelling medium.
sidequest-3.challenge: The main challenge was mixing two very different worlds without making the audio sound messy. In my first draft, the techno beats were too loud, which made the grocery store sounds hard to hear and caused the different layers to clash with each other.
sidequest-3.client: Minor Audio & Visual Design, Hogeschool Utrecht
sidequest-3.process: To begin, I brainstormed all possible sounds present in a grocery store in particular Albert Heijn, categorizing them into groups such as those associated with the physical environment, sounds generated by humans or devices, and ambient sounds. I followed the same procedure for the sounds found in a techno club. The subsequent step involved planning the beginning, middle, and end points of the sound journey. I conceived the idea of conducting a walkthrough with sounds through an Albert Heijn store because the layout of every store follows a similar concept: fresh products like fruits and veggies come first, followed by the refrigerator section and bakery items. It then transitions to the aisle sections for dry products, followed by the drinks and freezers towards the end, ending at the cashier. At the end I changed this idea a little bit and mixed the grocery errands with an activity which is very known for the techno scene. Due experimenting with the audio the idea with the walkthrough I turned the concept into entering the club/ah store, looking for the goods and experiencing the goods/being at the cashier checkout.

processImages.caption: Ableton Live snapshot showing layered supermarket and techno sounds, with applied effects and automation.

sidequest-3.results: The final result is an immersive audio piece that reframes a shopping trip as an electronic listening experience. The project expanded my use of production techniques such as auto-filters and sidechaining to shape texture, pacing, and clarity. It also strengthened my ability to build narrative and mood through sound design alone.

sidequest-4.title: IKEA Kvartett
sidequest-4.subtitle: A playful collectible card game bringing store culture and iconic product moments into a take-home game.
sidequest-4.description: Working part time in logistics at IKEA Utrecht gave me a good overview of store culture. I noticed how much visitors love items that are central to the store experience but cannot officially be taken home, like the iconic yellow shopping bags. This sparked a question: what if customers could collect those store-only artifacts and iconic products as a physical game to take home?
sidequest-4.challenge: How might we translate the quirks, store navigation, and favorite products of an IKEA trip into a physical souvenir that feels authentic to the brand and fun to play?
sidequest-4.process: Over a one-week creative sprint, I designed a traditional Quartet card game using IKEA's distinct visual language. I categorized products alongside store-only elements (like yellow bags, food court items or all time favs), using clean graphic hierarchy, custom iconography, and brand-accurate typography so the cards feel genuinely 'IKEA-coded.'
sidequest-4.results: This self-initiated project showcases creative initiative and how everyday workplace observations can spark fun design concepts. It highlights my ability to capture brand identity, apply visual hierarchy, and design lighthearted interactions driven by real human observation.
